answer_json.answer: The right to buy at the strike

lesson_text: The right to buy NVDA at the strike, and that's it. You don't own a single share. You own a contract, good until expiry, and nothing forces you to use it. The obligation sits with whoever sold you the call. If you exercise, they have to sell. That's what makes a bought call defined risk. The premium you paid is the most you can lose, so the premium is your stop. We trade shares most of the time. A call is the occasional defined-risk alternative, not the default. A call is a right to buy. Whether you use it is up to you.

An obligation to buy at the strike

lesson_text: The one on the jumpy stock. Both calls are at the money, 100 on 100, so neither has any intrinsic value. The whole difference is time value. A stock that swings 5% most days has a real shot at a big move before expiry, and you pay for that chance up front. All else equal, bigger expected swings raise call and put prices alike. The down days don't cancel the up days in the price. So on a fast-moving leader, expect the calls to look expensive. That's the movement you're paying for. Fast movers carry fat time value. You pay for the movement up front.

lesson_text: How much the delta changes. Delta is about how much your option moves for each $1 in the stock. Gamma is how much that delta itself shifts on the same $1. Think of delta as your speed and gamma as your acceleration. Here's why you care. With a lot of gamma, your option doesn't move at one steady pace. Own it, and each dollar your way pays a bit more than the last. Theta and vega have their own columns: time decay and implied volatility. Delta is your speed. Gamma is how fast that speed changes.

depth.summary: A cash-secured put is a sold put with enough cash set aside to buy the shares. A put is cash-secured when the writer deposits cash equal to the strike price. A cash-secured put seller sets aside enough cash to buy the shares if assigned. Unlike a naked put writer, the cash-secured writer has the money set aside and welcomes assignment. A cash-secured put can still lose money if the stock falls. One standard contract covers 100 shares. Only sell the put at a strike you'd own the stock at, however low it goes.

reveal_json.lesson_line: Cash-secured means the money to buy the shares is parked the day the put is sold.
reveal_json.simple: He sold a put and set the cash aside to buy the shares at the strike if he's assigned.
reveal_json.why: He sold the put and parked the cash to buy the shares. That put can make him buy 100 shares at the strike, so the cash covers the strike times 100 for each contract. If he's assigned, that money pays for the stock. Here's what people miss. The cash only means he can pay. It doesn't make the trade safe. If ZQRT keeps falling, he still buys at the strike and the loss is his. He'd better want that stock at that price, however far it drops. That's the seller's side, not our trade.

wrong.He sold a put on shares he owns: A sold put can make him buy shares, not sell them. Shares he holds don't pay for that. Cash does.
wrong.He sold a put with no cash behind it: Then it isn't cash-secured. The money's set aside before any assignment shows up.

depth.summary: Pin risk is the writer's risk that the stock finishes right at the strike on expiry. With a pinned short, you may find an unexpected stock position on Monday. The only way to avoid assignment on a given day is to close the short before that day's close. Buying stock in advance of an expected assignment can leave you unexpectedly long on Monday if the assignment never comes. Near the strike at expiry, either close the position early or be ready for either outcome Monday. The not-knowing is worst when the stock sits right around the short strike. Options in the money by $0.01 or more at the close are typically exercised automatically; holders can decide until 4:30 p.m. Central. Expiring PM-settled options typically stop trading at the 3 p.m. Central close, some ETF options a little later. Under FINRA's rule, holders have until 5:30 p.m. ET on expiry day to make the final exercise decision. In the select stocks Cboe opens to extended hours, expiring options can trade until 4:15 p.m. ET on expiry day. OCC decides whether an expiring stock option is in the money from the stock's 4:00 p.m. ET close. Each stock option contract covers 100 shares.

reveal_json.lesson_line: Right at the strike on expiry day, close the short. Guessing is how you get a Monday surprise.

lesson_text: Exercise the 55 puts himself, and fast. Holders of the 50 puts can still exercise tonight. So he can be assigned shares at 50 with the stock at 40. His 55s closed out of the money at 56, so automatic exercise skips them. Nobody does it for him. Exercise them before his broker's cut-off, and he sells at 55, which keeps the spread's gain. Skip it and they expire, and he's stuck with shares bought at 50 and nothing under them. That's FINRA's own example. You should know your broker's cut-off before you ever need it. After-hours news can flip an expiring spread. Know your broker's cut-off, and be ready to exercise the long leg yourself.

reveal_json.simple: It buys shares. The sold calls are short delta, and owning stock cancels that out.
reveal_json.why: It buys shares. Selling those calls leaves the market maker short delta. If the stock rips, the calls cost it money. Stock it owns is long delta, so buying shares cancels that out. wrong.Waits and buys shares at expiry: The sold calls carry short delta from the minute they're sold. The hedge goes on as the stock moves, not at the end.

lesson_text: Closes cluster near strike prices. Ni, Pearson and Poteshman found stocks with listed options tend to finish right at strikes on expiration dates. They measured returns moved by at least 16.5 basis points on average, each expiration. They tied it to market makers rebalancing hedges, plus manipulation by prop traders. That's an average across a lot of stocks, though. It's a tendency, not a call on where yours closes Friday. Strikes can act like magnets into expiry. A tendency, not a promise.

depth.summary: Volume is one session's trading; open interest is the running total of contracts still open. Open interest depends on whether each side opened or closed, and OCC reports the new figure only after the day ends. Both sides opening raises open interest. Both sides closing lowers open interest. One side opening and the other closing leaves open interest unchanged: the position changes hands. Exercised and assigned contracts are closed too, so they also come out of open interest. Every open contract has a buyer and a seller behind it, so it carries both views at once. Unusual options activity is neither bullish nor bearish by default. Unusual volume isn't bullish by default; it can just be a large investor hedging. Outsiders can barely see who bought, who sold, and who opened or closed.

facts.given: A call's volume today is three times its open interest, and your flow screen lights it up. What do you know for sure? Heavy trading versus what was open Open interest will rise next day New buyers opened bullish calls The stock is about to move a lot

reveal_json.lesson_line: Volume over open interest means heavy trading, not proof of new bets.
reveal_json.simple: Just that a lot traded compared with what was open. Volume can't show how much was new.
reveal_json.why: Only that it traded heavy compared with what was open. Volume is today. Open interest is what was already out there. Some of today's trades may have closed positions, and some just changed hands. Even the next count only shows the net change, so it can't tell you how many were new. Treat a flag like that as a reason to pull up the chart and do the homework. It isn't a buy signal on its own.

wrong.New buyers opened bullish calls: You can't see who opened or closed, and every contract has a seller on the other side.
wrong.Open interest will rise next day: Not for sure. It rises only from trades where both sides open, and falls from trades where both close. Volume can't show that mix.
wrong.The stock is about to move a lot: Heavy volume says people traded it, not what the stock does next. It can be hedges, closes or bets.

answer_json.answer: Whether he'll be assigned the stock

lesson_text: Whether he gets assigned. That's pin risk. The stock finishes right on the strike, and the seller can't know how many of his puts get assigned. If he's assigned, he starts the next session long the stock, a position he never planned. And it can move against him by the next open. That's the seller's side, not ours. When we buy an option now and then, the premium we pay is the stop. Short an option into expiry with the stock sitting on the strike: that's pin risk.

sources.name: The Options Industry Council (OCC): Options Glossary (P): Pin risk
sources.quote: The risk to an investor (option writer) that the stock price will exactly equal the strike price at expiration (that option will be exactly at-the-money). … The investor will not know how many of their written(short) options will be assigned … The risk is that on the following Monday the option writer might have an unexpected long (in the case of a written put) or short (in the case of a written call) stock position

depth.summary: Pin risk is the option seller's risk that the stock finishes exactly at the strike at expiration. With the stock on the strike, a seller can't know how many short options will be assigned. Pin risk can leave a seller with a surprise stock position after expiration: long from a short put, short from a short call.

facts.given: A friend sold a put at the 50 strike. The stock closes right at 50 on expiry day. What can't he know yet? Whether he'll be assigned the stock What strike he wrote the put at How much premium he collected Whether the put is in the money

reveal_json.lesson_line: Short an option into expiry with the stock sitting on the strike: that's pin risk.
reveal_json.simple: Whether he gets assigned. A close right on the strike leaves the seller guessing, and assignment means stock he never planned on.
reveal_json.why: Whether he gets assigned. That's pin risk. The stock finishes right on the strike, and the seller can't know how many of his puts get assigned. If he's assigned, he starts the next session long the stock, a position he never planned. And it can move against him by the next open. That's the seller's side, not ours. When we buy an option now and then, the premium we pay is the stop.

wrong.How much premium he collected: The premium hit his account when he sold. The open question is assignment.
wrong.What strike he wrote the put at: He knows his own strike. It's 50. What he doesn't know is assignment.
wrong.Whether the put is in the money: With the stock right on 50, it isn't in the money. The unknown is whether it gets assigned anyway.

steps: Market makers, the dealers, take the other side of public orders. Then they hedge with stock to stay neutral.
The theory: long gamma, their hedging sells rallies and buys dips. Short gamma, they chase the move.
